extracted.intended_audience: people who need to write press releases (PR pros, small business owners, nonprofit communicators, beginners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing a news-style press release that journalists can use with minimal editing, including headline, lead, body, boilerplate, contact info, formatting, and distribution tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a genuine headline
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be brief, clear and to the point: an ultra-compact version of the press release’s key point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The headline is the eye-catcher; many PR professionals recommend writing it after the release is drafted. Use present tense, exclude 'a' and 'the' and some forms of 'to be'. First word capitalized; avoid capitalizing every word. Bold and larger font is conventional. A grabber headline attracts journalists; use the headline as the email subject line if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract important keywords for visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract the most important keywords from your press release and use them early in the headline and summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using keywords early gives better search engine visibility and makes it simpler for journalists and readers to get the idea. If including a summary sentence after the headline, apply the same rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the body copy as you want it to appear in a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Most journalists will use much of your release in their writeup, so write it in a news-like manner and include the details you want reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making journalists do extensive research—include facts you want included. If it doesn't sound credible, journalists may dig deeper; keep it credible and ready-for-press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the date and city
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the release body with the date and the city the release originates from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city may be omitted if confusing (e.g., written in New York about events in Chicago). The first paragraph should sum up the news and may start with the date or where the news is coming from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead sentence should be a concise summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead (first sentence) should grab the reader and concisely state what is happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first paragraph (two to three sentences) should sum up the release; the next one to two sentences should then expand upon the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate the 5 W's (and the H) clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer who, what, when, where, why, and how so the reader has everything they need to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to ensure basics are defined (e.g., who is this about, what is the news, when does it happen, where, why it's newsworthy, how it's happening). Fill gaps with information about people, products, dates and related details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the copy compact and economical
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid very long sentences and paragraphs, repetition, jargon, and wasted words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for simplicity and no wasted words; make concrete factual statements (events, products, people, dates, goals). If the start doesn't generate interest, readers likely won't finish the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it clean, crisp, and applicable to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the release is as close to 'ready for press' as possible and targeted to the right audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors decide quickly whether your piece is worth publishing; poor grammar, missing basics, or fluff will get ignored. Ask why the audience should care and tailor the news to that market's definition of 'newsworthy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide supporting links and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Include extra information links that support the press release (company pages, media pages, press kits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the company has additional online information or a media page, add the exact URL (not 'click here') so it prints clearly and is useful to journalists. Tie to relevant online resources like PR Web or PR Newswire when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the standard document structure and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include standard elements: 'FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE' (or EMBARGOED UNTIL...), headline, optional subhead, lead paragraph, secondary paragraphs, boilerplate, contact info, and multimedia handles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embargoed, write 'EMBARGOED UNTIL...' with the date. Headline usually centered and in bold; subhead in italics if used. First paragraph = most important info; second/third paragraphs = quotes and facts. Signal end with three # symbols centered under last line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a boilerplate 'About [Company]'
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an 'About' section with information describing the company, its core business and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title it 'About [XYZ_COMPANY]' and use a paragraph or two (5–6 lines each) explaining who you are, achievements, mission. Point to the company's exact media or website URL at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete, specific contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact details for the media/PR person or another appointed contact who will be available after release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact details must be limited and specific to the current release and should include: company's official name; media department's official name and contact person; office address; telephone and fax numbers with country/city codes and extensions; mobile (optional); times of availability; email addresses; website address. If providing other people's contact details, get their agreement and ensure availability at reasonable hours following the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep releases to one page when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut the release to length — it should be a page long at most in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are unlikely to spend time on long releases unless covering very major events; be succinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a clear, on-brand quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Always include a quote—ideally from the lead individual involved— that expands on the significance and allows journalists to prepare a complete article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quote need not be an actual spoken quote but should be plausible; confirm the quoted person is happy with it. A quote lets busy journalists complete stories without follow-up interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal the end with three # symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three hash symbols (###) centered under the last line to mark the end of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a journalistic standard indicating the end of the copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper style and good grammar (ready-for-press standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP or newsroom style and ensure accurate grammar; avoid fluff and advertising copy that editors will delete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make life easier for editing teams by writing close to the way the editor will publish it. Avoid over-the-top promotional language; place descriptive company language in the boilerplate and keep it factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid negative or investigatory phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep releases upbeat and positive; avoid phrasing that invites investigation ('following the resignation', 'after a period of inactivity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative ways of wording situations can prompt journalists to investigate or emphasize sensitive angles you may not want covered. Frame circumstances neutrally and positively when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the email subject 'press release'
rubrics_metrics.description: When emailing a press release, use your grabber headline as the email subject rather than 'press release'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject like 'press release' blends into crowded inboxes; a specific attention-getting subject increases the chance of being opened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send releases at times that increase pickup likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Send in the morning when possible so editors have time to work your piece into their day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being considerate of an editor's schedule increases the chance of coverage; morning distribution gives more opportunity for pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a call to action when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want the public to take action (buy, visit website, enter contest), include clear instructions and where to do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify where the product is available, a website address, phone number, or other action details so readers know what to do next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multimedia and social handles where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Add links or handles for Twitter and other multimedia assets to aid online coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern releases often include social media handles or multimedia references to make it easy for digital coverage and sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep contact details specific to the current release
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact details should refer only to the people and resources relevant to this particular release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not recycle generic or outdated contact info; appoint a specific person if no media team exists and ensure they are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: If embargoed, state embargo details clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Put 'EMBARGOED UNTIL...' with the date you want the story released when you do not want immediate distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A release with no release date is presumed to be for immediate release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep factual, verifiable content and avoid promotional fluff
rubrics_metrics.description: Deal with actual facts — events, products, services, people, targets, goals, plans, projects — and provide maximum use of concrete facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluffy advertising copy or unverifiable claims reduce credibility and the likelihood of pickup; stick to facts journalists can use and verify.
